name: Andrej Karpathy
shortDescription: Neural networks built from an empty file, one two-hour lecture at a time, by someone who did this work at the top of the field.
longDescription: Seventeen uploads, thirteen of them over eight minutes, median a hundred and fifteen. There is no filler here at all. The spine is the Zero to Hero sequence: backpropagation built from scratch in micrograd, then language modelling built up across five makemore parts, then GPT written line by line, then a tokenizer, then GPT-2 reproduced at 124 million parameters across four hours. Nothing is imported that has not first been built. Alongside it sit two long orientation pieces — a one-hour introduction to large language models and a three-and-a-half-hour deep dive aimed at people who use them rather than train them — and a separate, more practical hundred-and-thirty-minute video on how he actually uses these tools day to day. Uploads are rare and the most recent in the scanned window is February 2025.
notFor: Anyone in a hurry, and anyone without comfortable Python and some calculus. These are lectures, not tutorials — the shortest useful one is an hour.

categories.why: Every abstraction is built before it is used — backpropagation, then a language model, then a transformer, then a tokenizer — which is the only way the later engineering decisions stop being guesswork.
categories.evidence: The Zero to Hero sequence: micrograd and backpropagation from scratch (146m), five makemore parts building up language modelling (76–118m each), GPT written from scratch (116m), the tokenizer (134m), and GPT-2 reproduced at 124M parameters (241m).

entryVideo.title: The spelled-out intro to neural networks and backpropagation: building micrograd
entryVideo.whyThisOne: The foundation everything else in the series stands on, built from nothing in one sitting. If this lands, the rest of the sequence is worth clearing time for.

categories.why: A separate strand aimed at people who use these systems rather than train them — different videos entirely from the from-scratch series, and unusually candid about what the tools are bad at.
categories.evidence: A 131-minute account of how he personally uses large language models day to day, a 60-minute general introduction for non-specialists, and a 211-minute deep dive on how the systems behave and why.

entryVideo.title: How I use LLMs
entryVideo.whyThisOne: Practice rather than theory, from someone who knows exactly how the machine works — which makes the limitations he names more credible than most advice on this subject.

caveats: Uploads are infrequent and the most recent in the scanned window is February 2025, so tooling specifics have moved. The from-scratch approach is superb for understanding and is not how anyone ships production systems.

name: Jack Herrington
shortDescription: Current React and frontend architecture explained at ten minutes a time, including which new things are not worth adopting.
longDescription: Sixty-nine long-form videos in two hundred uploads, median around eight minutes, and the subject is the frontend as it currently is rather than as it was when a course was recorded — React Server Components and partial caching, the React compiler, new hooks assessed rather than announced. The useful habit is scepticism: one video asks whether a new hook is a genuine improvement or a gimmick and answers it, which is rarer than it should be in a field whose content economy rewards enthusiasm. He goes deep on specific libraries too, including a hundred-minute session on one ecosystem. Some recent uploads have drifted toward AI tooling, but the frontend material is current and is still the bulk of it.
notFor: Beginners — this assumes React is already familiar and you are trying to keep up rather than start. Framework-specific and moves fast, so older videos date quickly.

categories.why: Keeps pace with a field that changes faster than any course can, and judges new features rather than announcing them — which is the skill this category actually needs.
categories.evidence: Videos on React Server Components and partial page caching, the React compiler, and an assessment of a new hook framed explicitly as improvement-or-gimmick, plus long-form on state and data libraries.

entryVideo.title: Partial Page Caching Using React Server Components
entryVideo.whyThisOne: A concrete current technique explained in nine minutes, which is a fair sample of both the depth and the pace.

caveats: Sponsored segments are frequent and several recent videos are built around AI developer tools. Highly React-specific: little here transfers to other frameworks, and the fast-moving subject means anything over a year old should be checked.
